title: Field Safety
text: This SOP covers field-based research activities and class field trips, addressing transportation, weather-based, and biotic hazards. Although we cannot predict all risks and hazards, it is everyone’s responsibility to identify and mitigate potential risks associated with field work.

title: Field Safety
text:
2 2. Scope

Applies to: All field-based research activities, class field trips, and off-campus data collection
Does not apply to: Laboratory-only procedures (see relevant Lab SOPs)
Location: All field sites used by the EA Program

title: Field Safety
text:
3 3. Responsibilities







Role
Responsibility




Instructor / PI
Approve field plans, ensure training compliance


Trained Personnel
Follow this SOP, report deviations and hazards


New Students
Complete training and document review before field work



Anyone conducting research in the field is required to have documented training before commencing field work. Learning about risks and taking the precautions described here is the first step to reducing the risks associated with field work. Anyone working in the field should identify potential risks and attempt to mitigate them.

title: Field Safety
text:
4 4. Safety and Hazards






WarningGeneral Field Hazards



Reducing risks is one of our main priorities. Like many endeavors in life, field work has certain risks. However, we can reduce these risks dramatically by understanding our physical limits and how these can be tested by uncontrolled environmental factors.
We rely on each individual to be mindful of their own limitations and to advocate for themselves and others to reduce risk exposure.



4.1 Required Materials

First Aid Kit (kits are located in EA vehicles; see EA vehicle checklist to document their presence)
Cell phone(s)
Walkie-talkies (optional)
Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)



4.2 Estimated Time
Preparing to go in the field can take a few minutes to several hours of planning and gathering resources. A good rule of thumb is to double the time you think it will take to get ready.

title: Field Safety
text:
5 5. Transportation Safety

5.1 5.1 Vehicle Requirements

Drivers must have valid driver’s licenses and insurance
Drivers using EA vehicles must be approved by the college; forms can be found in the EA Department



5.2 5.2 Planning

Identify meet-up and departure times and locations
Designate a driver
All state and local laws must be obeyed



5.3 5.3 Responding to Vehicle Emergencies
Refer to the college’s vehicle emergency procedures. Ensure all occupants are safe, call emergency services if needed, and report the incident to the EA Department.

title: Field Safety
text:
6 6. Weather-Related Hazards

6.1 6.1 Heat Exhaustion and Stroke






WarningRisk Factors




Working outside of shade in desert or arid climates, especially during hot times of day
Lack of shade coverage or proper sun protection
Dehydration



Prevention:

Use and reapply sunscreen
Drink plenty of water
Wear hats and other protective clothing

Response:

Hydrate the affected person
Place ice packs on neck, armpits, etc.
If conditions worsen, leave the field and find air-conditioned conditions



6.2 6.2 Cold Conditions
Risk factors: Lack of sun, time of year, wind chill
Prevention: Proper layering and clothing; stay hydrated
Response: Eat, evacuate to warmth, get a professional evaluation


6.3 6.3 Lightning
Prevention: Check weather forecast; learn to identify cumulonimbus clouds
Response: Assume lightning position and seek shelter immediately; avoid open areas, tall isolated trees, and bodies of water


6.4 6.4 Air Quality and Pollution
Working outside when ozone levels or other pollutants are elevated has a detrimental effect on health, particularly for individuals with asthma or other respiratory conditions. Hot, dry days worsen pollution, and nearby forest fires degrade air quality.
Students with any respiratory disease should be cautious and report the condition to their instructor or laboratory supervisor.
Prevention: Check air quality index (AQI) before field work; postpone if AQI is unhealthy
Response: Leave the field if symptoms develop; seek medical attention if needed

title: Field Safety
text:
7 7. Geological and Environmental Hazards

7.1 7.1 Earthquake
Tectonic movement may occur anywhere in California.
Prevention: Be aware of surroundings at all times
Response: Remain low to the ground; stay away from external building frames; avoid sinkholes, gas lines, and utility wires


7.2 7.2 Flooding
Risk factors: Proximity to bodies of water, excessive rainfall
Prevention: Check the forecast for rainfall; be aware of surroundings
Response: Find the highest point in the area; do not attempt to cross rushing water


7.3 7.3 Altitude Illness (HAPE/HACE)
Risk factors: High altitudes to which students have not had time to acclimate; reduced oxygen
Symptoms: Headache, nausea, irritability
Response: If mild symptoms, acclimate and take it easy; hydrate. If persistent vomiting and severe headache, evacuate to lower altitude immediately.


7.4 7.4 Human Debris and Waste
Illegal dumping of waste and leftover construction materials (sharp metallic objects, etc.) bring risk of injury and exposure to long-term illnesses like tetanus.
Prevention: Avoid and report; be aware of surroundings; think before interacting with unusual objects
Response: Students should be aware of their vaccination history and how to proceed if they require a tetanus shot due to injury


7.5 7.5 Toxic Waste Exposure
Exposure may occur via ingestion, inhalation, or dermal contact and can be unpredictable.
Prevention: Wear appropriate PPE; avoid contact with unknown substances
Response: Remove from exposure; decontaminate; seek medical attention

title: Field Safety
text:
8 8. Biotic Hazards
The field is home to a vast diversity of organisms. Being respectful of their environment is crucial to their safety and our own.

8.1 8.1 Allergies






Important



All allergies must be recorded in medical files before the start of field work. Researchers with life-threatening allergies must bring their Epi-pen to the field and keep it accessible at all times.


Mild allergic reaction: Administer 25–50 mg of Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
Severe allergic reaction (swelling of face/throat, respiratory distress): Administer 0.3 mg of Epinephrine; may re-administer after 5 minutes. Follow with 25–50 mg of Diphenhydramine and 20–40 mg of Prednisone. Evacuate from field site immediately.


8.2 8.2 Biotic Risk Summary









Organism
Habitats
Risks
Prevention and Response




Mosquitos
Near stagnant water
Vectors for disease (e.g., Malaria)
Use mosquito repellent (e.g., DEET products)


Rodents
Debris, dense underbrush, burrow holes
Disease, infection
Do not touch rodents; if bitten, clean and disinfect


Mountain Lions
Native to North/South America; active early and late in the day
Severe injury
Make yourself look larger; do not run; throw rocks or sticks; avoid being alone


Snakes (Rattlesnakes, Cottonmouth)
Various
Snakebite
Walk in open areas; wear heavy boots; listen for rattle; back away slowly; if bitten, seek immediate medical attention


Spiders (Black Widow, Brown Recluse)
Dark sheltered areas
Spider bite, nausea
Wear gloves while working; shake out clothing and bedding; go to hospital if bitten


Bees and Wasps
Various
Swelling, pain, allergic reaction, anaphylactic shock
Avoid disturbing nests; stay calm when pursued; administer epinephrine for severe reactions; take to hospital


Fleas and Ticks
Underbrush, wooded areas
Lyme disease
Tick check after fieldwork; use insect repellent; wear long clothing; suffocate tick with petroleum jelly before removing with tweezers


Poison Oak
Riparian habitats
Itchy rash; red, swollen skin
Learn to identify; apply Tecnu beforehand; wash affected areas with dish soap


Stinging Nettle
Riparian habitats, meadows
Stinging sensation
Learn to identify and avoid; use anti-itch cream if needed

title: Field Safety
text:
9 9. Other Illness and Injury

9.1 9.1 Fractures and Breaks
Stabilize the injured area and avoid movement. Go to the nearest medical facility for further care.


9.2 9.2 Injury from Equipment
Handle all equipment with caution. Carefully read operating procedures. Seek help from fellow students or your instructor if you have questions or doubts. Do not use any equipment if you are unsure of how to handle it.


9.3 9.3 Chronic Conditions (Epilepsy, Diabetes, Heart Conditions)
Refer to emergency procedures. Report any chronic conditions to your supervisor. Be aware of your surroundings and be prepared to react in an emergency. Know where the first aid kit is and how to get to the nearest medical facility.

11 11. Emergency Response Procedure

11.1 11.1 Responding to a Medical Emergency

Survey the scene
Identify any potential risks that could affect other team members
Do not move the injured person unless necessary

Suspected type of injury or illness

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
text:
R, RStudio, and GitHub combine as a resource for data analysis, display, and collaboration. This SOP provides instructions to create RStudio projects, connect them to GitHub repositories, and manage collaborative workflows using version control.
We do not expect you to be an expert on R or RStudio. However, some experience with a computer language will be helpful.

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
text:
2. Scope

Applies to: All EA Program researchers using R for data analysis and collaborative projects
Does not apply to: Local-only R scripts with no version control requirements; Python or other language workflows
Location: RStudio Server (Pomona College) or local installations

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
text:
3. Acknowledgements
The following have made substantial contributions to this SOP: Aparna Chintapalli. As always, we acknowledge the students who have tried to follow these instructions and made suggestions for improvement. If you have suggestions or edits, please let the authors know.

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
text:
4. Definitions
RStudio: The user interface for R. While R itself is a free programming environment with a robust range of statistical packages, RStudio provides tools to track and publish analysis in an efficient and transparent way.
Local Install vs. Server: R and RStudio can be installed on a local computer from the CRAN download mirror sites. We also have access to the RStudio Server installed on the Pomona College mainframe, accessible via a web browser.
GitHub: A web-based Git repository hosting service for collaborative code and document management.
Version Control: A method to track changes in software, especially in collaborative projects. RStudio projects and GitHub repositories can be shared among collaborators, with contributions tracked via version control tools.

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
text:
5. Why R + RStudio + GitHub?
These tools together enable four key principles:
Collaboration: You can easily collaborate with others and track who contributed to various parts of the repository. When working in a team and updating text and code, version control ensures you can trace how things changed.
Transparency: Others can see how you analyzed data, providing clear access to your methods.
Reproducibility: When you conduct an analysis, you can reproduce the results, which validates your findings.
Accessibility: Accessible from any computer via the web server. Because we can rely on consistent behavior and web-based servers, operating systems and hardware rarely limit what you can do in R.






Note



Becoming experienced with these programs is like learning to walk. We need to approach this in discrete steps. Some people will experience weeks of mistakes before feeling confident; others will learn quickly. How fast you get comfortable depends on many factors but will be greatly improved by the time you invest.

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
text:
6. Interferences

R is updated approximately every six months. Occasionally, new versions will no longer run older code, requiring maintenance of older versions. This almost never affects new users.
RStudio Server needs a functional network connection. If the network is down, the server is inaccessible.

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
text:
7. Health and Safety

Risk of carpal tunnel syndrome from extended computer use. Maintain good posture and a well-designed workstation.
Frustration is common! After running into baffling errors, go for a run, get dinner, or take a nap. You’ll often find a workaround after taking a break.

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub

Laptop or desktop computer
Access to Pomona College’s SSO (single sign-on) and server
GitHub account (free at github.com)
Patience

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
text:
10. Introducing RStudio

10.1 RStudio Server Login
The RStudio Server is hosted by Pomona College, so you need a Pomona College login. Non-Pomona students need a new login each semester, obtainable from the help desk at Cowart Information Technology Services.
Server addresses:

On Pomona’s network (or VPN): rstudio.campus.pomona.edu
Off campus / non-Pomona networks: rstudio.pomona.edu



From non-Pomona networks you may get a privacy error. If so, go to Advanced and accept the privacy settings to continue.





10.2 The Four RStudio Panels
Working with RStudio can be confusing at first. Here are the four default panels:
Upper Left – Text and Code Editor: This panel displays your text files (.Rnw, .Rmd, .R, .tex, .txt). If no file is open, this panel won’t appear and the console takes the entire left side. Close files you’re not actively editing to avoid confusion.
Lower Left – Console: The R console where you enter commands directly or submit them from the editor above. Errors are displayed in red here. If you compile a LaTeX file, the log appears here too.
Lower Right – Files/Plots/Packages/Help: Shows your workspace files, installed packages, plots, and help documentation. If a plot is too large for the window, resize the panel.
Upper Right – Environment/History/Git: The Environment tab shows objects R has access to. The History tab displays your command history. The Git tab manages files between GitHub and your local/server directory.








TipTip



To see all four panels, create a new text file: File > New File > R Sweave. Save it as “Test.Rnw” and all four panels will appear.

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
section: 11. Setting Up Accounts and SSH Keys
text:
11. Setting Up Accounts and SSH Keys

11.1 Create a GitHub Account

Go to github.com and create an account
Use your Claremont email address – this helps later if you want free private repositories for students at education.github.com
For our purposes you will not need a private repository initially



11.2 Configure RStudio for knitr

In RStudio, navigate to Tools > Global Options > Sweave
Change the “Weave Rnw files” option from Sweave to knitr
Apply and close



11.3 Create an SSH Key in RStudio

Open RStudio (server or local)
Navigate to Tools > Global Options > Git/SVN
Click “Create SSH Key”
Select “RSA” under SSH Key Type
Leave the passphrase blank for now (add one later for extra security on sensitive projects)
Click “Create” – a pop-up image will appear (an encryption visualization; close it)
Click “View public key” and copy the contents with Ctrl-C






11.4 Add the SSH Key to GitHub

Go to your GitHub profile (upper right corner of any GitHub page)
Select “Settings”
In the left menu, select “SSH and GPG keys”
Click “New SSH key”
Type a name (e.g., “myRStudio SSH key”)
Paste the RSA key from your clipboard into the key field
Click the green “Add SSH key” button

GitHub and RStudio can now communicate.

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
section: 12. Linking an RStudio Project to a GitHub Repository
text:
12. Linking an RStudio Project to a GitHub Repository

12.1 Clone a Repository
We will use a practice repository called beginnersluck (search GitHub for it under the username marclos).

On the GitHub repository page, click the green “Code” button



Select “Clone with SSH” – IMPORTANT: if the header says “Clone with HTTPS,” click the small “Use SSH” link to toggle. If you skip this step, the project is very hard to fix afterward.



Copy the SSH URL to your clipboard



12.2 Create an RStudio Project from the Clone

In RStudio, go to File > New Project
Select “Version Control”



Select “Git”



Paste the SSH URL into the “Repository URL” field (Ctrl-V). The project directory name should auto-fill.
Click “Create Project”



If prompted about establishing authenticity, type yes and hit OK



You should now see the repository files in RStudio. If nothing appears, check if your pop-up blocker is active and disable it for this site.

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
section: 13. Daily Workflow: Pull, Edit, Commit, Push
text:
13. Daily Workflow: Pull, Edit, Commit, Push

13.1 Best Practices
Every time you sit down to work:

Pull first (blue downward arrow in the Git tab) to get the latest changes
Edit your files
Commit your changes (check the staged boxes, write a commit message)
Push your changes (green upward arrow) to share with collaborators






13.2 Pull Results
When you pull, you’ll get one of three results:
“Already up-to-date.” Your files have not been updated on GitHub since your last pull. If you expect changes from a collaborator, they may have forgotten to push.
Successful update. You’ll see a summary of files changed, insertions, and deletions.
Unsuccessful pull. You have local changes that conflict with remote changes. See Troubleshooting (Section 15).


13.3 Committing Changes

In the Git tab (upper right), check the boxes next to the files you want to commit



Click “Commit”
Write a meaningful commit message describing your changes
Click “Commit”



13.4 Push Results
“Everything up-to-date.” Nothing new to push.
Successful push. You’ll see a message like e2efe6f..0b18250 master -> master.
Unsuccessful push. See Troubleshooting (Section 15).

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
text:
14. Collaboration

14.1 Becoming a Collaborator
To contribute to someone else’s repository, they must add you as a collaborator. Send your GitHub username to the repository owner so they can add you via Settings > Collaborators in the repository.


14.2 Adding Collaborators to Your Repository

Go to your repository on GitHub
Click Settings in the toolbar
Click “Collaborators”
Add your collaborators’ GitHub usernames

title: RStudio Projects and GitHub
text:
15. Troubleshooting

15.1 Identity Error
If you receive an identity error, fix it using the Git shell. In the Git tab, click the gear icon and select “Shell…” Then type:
git config user.email "your.email@claremont.edu"
git config user.name "Your Name"


15.2 Merge Conflicts
Merge errors occur when you and a collaborator have both modified the same section of a file. To resolve:

In the Git tab, look for files with a “U” (unmerged) status
Open the conflicted file – you’ll see markers like <<<<<<< HEAD and >>>>>>> origin/main showing both versions
Edit the file to keep the correct content and remove the conflict markers
Save the file
Check the file’s box in the Git tab
Commit with a message like “Resolved merge conflict”
Push



15.3 “fatal: Not possible to fast-forward, aborting.”
Run this in the Git shell:
git pull --rebase


15.4 Pull is Rejected (Unmerged Files)
If you see “Pull is not possible because you have unmerged files,” you must resolve the merge conflicts first (see 15.2), then add and commit the changes before pulling again.


15.5 Divergent Branches
If you see “You have divergent branches and need to specify how to reconcile them,” run one of the following in the Git shell:
git config pull.rebase false   # merge (recommended for beginners)
Then try pulling again.


15.6 Non-Fast-Forward Errors
If another person has pushed to the same branch, Git won’t be able to push your changes. Fix by fetching and merging:
git fetch origin
git merge origin main
Or simply use git pull to perform both commands at once.


15.7 Nuclear Option: Deleting a Project
If you are willing to sacrifice your local changes (or have emailed them to a collaborator):

Delete all files in the project directory
Clear workspace and console (don’t save)
Go to Session > Terminate R
Start a new project by cloning the repository again (Section 12)

title: Soil Sampling and Processing
text:
6. Procedure

6.1 Pre-Sampling Preparation

Develop a sampling plan that identifies the number of samples, locations, depths, and analyses to be performed
Pre-label all sample bags with site name, plot ID, date, depth, and collector initials
Calibrate the depth marker on the auger to 15 cm (or other target depth)
Clean all sampling equipment with deionized water and dry before use
Check that the cooler has sufficient ice packs for biological subsamples
File a field work planning form per SOP-F01



6.2 Field Sampling

Navigate to the predetermined sampling location and record GPS coordinates
Clear surface litter and debris from the sampling point without disturbing the mineral soil surface
Insert the soil auger vertically into the soil and advance to the target depth (0–15 cm)
Withdraw the auger carefully, keeping the soil core intact
Extrude the soil from the auger into a labeled sample bag using a clean trowel
For composite samples, combine cores from multiple locations within the same plot into a single bucket for homogenization
Mark the completed sampling location with a flag
Backfill the auger hole with surrounding soil to minimize site disturbance







TipTip



Do not sample saturated soils. If soils are waterlogged, note this in the field notebook and postpone sampling or adjust the protocol accordingly.




6.3 Decontamination Between Samples

Remove all visible soil from the auger and trowel
Rinse equipment with deionized water between plots (not between subsamples within the same composite)
Use a new pair of gloves when moving between experimental treatments to prevent cross-contamination



6.4 Sample Transport

Place samples for biological analysis (microbial biomass, soil respiration) into the cooler immediately after collection
Transport all samples to the laboratory as soon as possible, ideally the same day
Record transport time and conditions in the field notebook



6.5 Laboratory Processing

Transfer each sample to a clean mixing tray
Homogenize the sample by hand, breaking up clods and mixing thoroughly
Pass the entire sample through a 2 mm sieve to remove coarse fragments (roots, rocks, gravel)
Record the mass of coarse fragments removed, if required by the analysis plan
Subdivide the sieved soil into labeled containers for each planned analysis



6.6 Storage Conditions








Analysis Type
Storage
Holding Time




Biological assays (MBC, respiration)
4 C, field-moist
Process within 48 hours

Indefinite once dry

Analyze extracts promptly


Archival
Air-dry, store in sealed bags at room temp
Indefinite









Important



Subsamples for biological assays must be stored at 4 C and processed within 48 hours of collection. Do not freeze biological subsamples unless the analysis protocol explicitly permits it.

7. Interferences






ImportantCritical Contamination Prevention



The inner surfaces of sample bottles and caps must not be touched with bare hands, gloves, or any other material. Sample bottles must be kept in a clean environment away from dust, dirt, fumes, and grime.



All sampling equipment must be clean and free of contaminants before use
Use only the recommended type of sample bottle for each parameter
Water sample bottles must be used for water samples only; never reuse bottles that have held concentrated reagents
Before field use, all preservatives must be tested and glassware spot-tested for cleanliness
The sample collector should keep hands clean and refrain from smoking while handling samples
Petroleum products (gasoline, oil, exhaust fumes) are prime sources of contamination; remove spills immediately
Exhaust fumes and cigarette smoke can contaminate samples with lead and other heavy metals
Air conditioning units are also a source of trace metal contamination
Solvent-rinsed Teflon or aluminum foil liners can prevent contamination from bottle caps for samples analyzed for organic compounds
Filter units must be kept clean (acid-washed, soaked in special solutions) and wrapped in solvent-rinsed aluminum foil
Sterilized bottles must remain sterile until sample collection; discard if the seal has been broken
All foreign and especially metal objects must be kept away from acids and water samples
Specific conductance should never be measured on water first used for pH measurements (KCl from the pH probe alters conductivity)

title: Surface Water Sampling
text:
8. Procedures

8.1 Preparation
Before sampling, the field investigator must:

Ensure sampling station locations and frequency are defined in the project design
Prepare accurate station location descriptions on the first visit to each site and follow them consistently on subsequent visits (temporal changes in water quality can only be interpreted with confidence if the same location is sampled each time)
Determine the hydrology and morphometrics (volume, depth, etc.) of the water body prior to sampling to identify phases, layers, flow patterns, and appropriate sample locations and depths
In impoundments, collect water quality profiles (dissolved oxygen, pH, temperature, conductivity, and ORP) at 1-meter intervals from substrate to surface to identify stratification

The selection of a sampling device depends on:

Whether the sample will be collected from shore or from a boat
The desired sampling depth
The overall depth and flow direction of the water body
The chemical nature of the analytes (floating vs. dissolved)



8.2 Field Collection – Direct Method

Remove the stopper or lid from the container just before sampling
Avoid contaminating the cap, neck, or inside of the bottle with fingers, wind-blown particles, or dripping water
If no preservative is present in the container: face upstream in flowing water and upwind in still water, hold the container near its base, reach out in front of your body, and plunge it mouth-down below the surface to approximately mid-water column
If the water is too shallow for this technique (risk of disturbing sediment), collect a surface water sample and note the change of method in the field notebook
Fill the bottle to the appropriate level for the analyte being tested
Pour out a small volume to create headspace for mixing in the lab, except for volatile organics and alkalinity samples (no headspace)



8.3 Field Collection – Extension Pole

Securely attach the sample container (with lid in place) to the pole holder using clamps or bands
Remove the container lid carefully to avoid contamination
Follow the direct method procedure above
Do not use this method for containers with preservative already present; use intermediate devices instead (Section 8.4)



8.4 Field Collection – Pre-Preserved Containers

Hold the container upright
Place the lid over the mouth so that only a small area forms an opening
Submerge and fill carefully to avoid loss of preservative



8.5 Field Collection – Intermediate Devices
For samples collected using Van Dorn, Kemmerer, bailers, or peristaltic pumps, follow the specific device operating instructions. Transfer collected water to the appropriate labeled sample containers promptly.






TipTip



Periodic “sampler blanks” consisting of ultrapure distilled water poured into or passed through the sampler should be prepared and submitted for laboratory analysis to verify sampler cleanliness.

title: Surface Water Sampling
text:
9. Sample Preservation, Handling, and Storage
Once samples have been collected:

Transfer the sample(s) into suitable labeled sample containers
Preserve the sample if appropriate, or verify that pre-preserved bottles were used
Record all pertinent data in the site logbook and on a field data sheet
Complete the chain of custody form
Attach custody seals to the cooler prior to shipment
Decontaminate all sampling equipment before collecting additional samples







Important



Samples must never be permitted to stand in the sun. Store samples on ice in coolers immediately after collection and ship to the laboratory without delay.

title: Surface Water Sampling
text:
10. Quality Control and Quality Assurance

Bottle Blanks
Prior to each field sampling trip, select one sample bottle per ten of each type being used, fill with ultrapure distilled water, preserve in the same manner as field samples, and submit with field samples for analysis as “bottle blanks.” This detects contamination from the bottle washing process.


Field Measurement Sub-Samples
Field measurements (pH, conductivity, temperature, DO) should always be made on a separate sub-sample, which is then discarded. Never make field measurements on the same water sample that will be returned to the laboratory for chemical analysis.


General Precautions

On the occasion that any procedure in this SOP is inappropriate, inadequate, or impractical and a variant procedure must be used, document the variant procedure and the circumstances requiring its use in the field logbook
Vehicle cleanliness is important for eliminating contamination; inspect and clean vehicles before transporting samples

title: Field Safety
text:
4. Safety and Hazards






WarningGeneral Field Hazards



Reducing risks is one of our main priorities. Like many endeavors in life, field work has certain risks. However, we can reduce these risks dramatically by understanding our physical limits and how these can be tested by uncontrolled environmental factors.
We rely on each individual to be mindful of their own limitations and to advocate for themselves and others to reduce risk exposure.



Required Materials

First Aid Kit (kits are located in EA vehicles; see EA vehicle checklist to document their presence)
Cell phone(s)
Walkie-talkies (optional)
Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)



Estimated Time
Preparing to go in the field can take a few minutes to several hours of planning and gathering resources. A good rule of thumb is to double the time you think it will take to get ready.

title: Field Safety
text:
5. Transportation Safety

5.1 Vehicle Requirements

Drivers must have valid driver’s licenses and insurance
Drivers using EA vehicles must be approved by the college; forms can be found in the EA Department



5.2 Planning

Identify meet-up and departure times and locations
Designate a driver
All state and local laws must be obeyed



5.3 Responding to Vehicle Emergencies
Refer to the college’s vehicle emergency procedures. Ensure all occupants are safe, call emergency services if needed, and report the incident to the EA Department.

title: Field Safety
text:
6. Weather-Related Hazards

6.1 Heat Exhaustion and Stroke






WarningRisk Factors




Working outside of shade in desert or arid climates, especially during hot times of day
Lack of shade coverage or proper sun protection
Dehydration



Prevention:

Use and reapply sunscreen
Drink plenty of water
Wear hats and other protective clothing

Response:

Hydrate the affected person
Place ice packs on neck, armpits, etc.
If conditions worsen, leave the field and find air-conditioned conditions



6.2 Cold Conditions
Risk factors: Lack of sun, time of year, wind chill
Prevention: Proper layering and clothing; stay hydrated
Response: Eat, evacuate to warmth, get a professional evaluation


6.3 Lightning
Prevention: Check weather forecast; learn to identify cumulonimbus clouds
Response: Assume lightning position and seek shelter immediately; avoid open areas, tall isolated trees, and bodies of water


6.4 Air Quality and Pollution
Working outside when ozone levels or other pollutants are elevated has a detrimental effect on health, particularly for individuals with asthma or other respiratory conditions. Hot, dry days worsen pollution, and nearby forest fires degrade air quality.
Students with any respiratory disease should be cautious and report the condition to their instructor or laboratory supervisor.
Prevention: Check air quality index (AQI) before field work; postpone if AQI is unhealthy
Response: Leave the field if symptoms develop; seek medical attention if needed

title: Field Safety
text:
7. Geological and Environmental Hazards

7.1 Earthquake
Tectonic movement may occur anywhere in California.
Prevention: Be aware of surroundings at all times
Response: Remain low to the ground; stay away from external building frames; avoid sinkholes, gas lines, and utility wires


7.2 Flooding
Risk factors: Proximity to bodies of water, excessive rainfall
Prevention: Check the forecast for rainfall; be aware of surroundings
Response: Find the highest point in the area; do not attempt to cross rushing water


7.3 Altitude Illness (HAPE/HACE)
Risk factors: High altitudes to which students have not had time to acclimate; reduced oxygen
Symptoms: Headache, nausea, irritability
Response: If mild symptoms, acclimate and take it easy; hydrate. If persistent vomiting and severe headache, evacuate to lower altitude immediately.


7.4 Human Debris and Waste
Illegal dumping of waste and leftover construction materials (sharp metallic objects, etc.) bring risk of injury and exposure to long-term illnesses like tetanus.
Prevention: Avoid and report; be aware of surroundings; think before interacting with unusual objects
Response: Students should be aware of their vaccination history and how to proceed if they require a tetanus shot due to injury


7.5 Toxic Waste Exposure
Exposure may occur via ingestion, inhalation, or dermal contact and can be unpredictable.
Prevention: Wear appropriate PPE; avoid contact with unknown substances
Response: Remove from exposure; decontaminate; seek medical attention

title: Field Safety
text:
8. Biotic Hazards
The field is home to a vast diversity of organisms. Being respectful of their environment is crucial to their safety and our own.

8.1 Allergies






Important



All allergies must be recorded in medical files before the start of field work. Researchers with life-threatening allergies must bring their Epi-pen to the field and keep it accessible at all times.


Mild allergic reaction: Administer 25–50 mg of Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
Severe allergic reaction (swelling of face/throat, respiratory distress): Administer 0.3 mg of Epinephrine; may re-administer after 5 minutes. Follow with 25–50 mg of Diphenhydramine and 20–40 mg of Prednisone. Evacuate from field site immediately.

9. Other Illness and Injury

9.1 Fractures and Breaks
Stabilize the injured area and avoid movement. Go to the nearest medical facility for further care.


9.2 Injury from Equipment
Handle all equipment with caution. Carefully read operating procedures. Seek help from fellow students or your instructor if you have questions or doubts. Do not use any equipment if you are unsure of how to handle it.


9.3 Chronic Conditions (Epilepsy, Diabetes, Heart Conditions)
Refer to emergency procedures. Report any chronic conditions to your supervisor. Be aware of your surroundings and be prepared to react in an emergency. Know where the first aid kit is and how to get to the nearest medical facility.

4. Safety and Hazards

Critical Safety Warning
Chloroform (CHCl3) is a volatile, toxic solvent and a suspected carcinogen. All fumigation steps must be performed inside a fume hood. Do not inhale chloroform vapors. Use ethanol-free chloroform only.


Hazards

Chemical: Chloroform (toxic, volatile); 0.5 M K2SO4 (mild irritant)
Physical: Vacuum desiccator under reduced pressure; glassware breakage



Required PPE

Nitrile gloves (double-glove recommended when handling chloroform)
Safety glasses or goggles
Lab coat
Work in fume hood at all times during fumigation



Emergency Procedures
In case of chloroform spill, refer to the SDS and SOP-L02 Hazardous Materials Handling. Evacuate the area if spill is large; ventilate the space and notify the supervisor.

title: Microbial Biomass Carbon – Chloroform Fumigation-Extraction
text:
6. Procedure

6.1 Preparation

Prepare 0.5 M K2SO4 by dissolving 87.1 g K2SO4 per liter of deionized water
Pre-combust glass fiber filters at 450 C for 4 hours and store in a clean container
Determine the gravimetric moisture content of a separate subsample (dry at 105 C for 24 hours) so results can be expressed on a dry-weight basis



6.2 Fumigation

Weigh two paired subsamples of 15 g field-moist soil into labeled extraction bottles
Place one set (fumigated) into the vacuum desiccator inside the fume hood
Place a beaker containing approximately 30 mL of ethanol-free chloroform and a few boiling chips in the center of the desiccator
Evacuate the desiccator using the vacuum pump until the chloroform begins to boil vigorously (approximately 2 minutes)
Close the stopcock and incubate in the dark at room temperature (approximately 25 C) for 24 hours
The second set (unfumigated controls) is extracted immediately (proceed to 6.3)



6.3 Extraction

After 24 hours, release the vacuum in the fume hood and remove the chloroform beaker
Evacuate the desiccator repeatedly (3–5 times) to remove residual chloroform vapor from the soil
Add 60 mL of 0.5 M K2SO4 to each bottle (both fumigated and unfumigated), achieving a 1:4 soil-to-extractant ratio
Cap bottles and shake on an orbital or end-over-end shaker for 1 hour
Allow the suspension to settle briefly, or centrifuge at 4000 x g for 10 minutes
Filter the supernatant through a pre-combusted 0.45 um glass fiber filter into a clean sample vial
Store filtered extracts at 4 C if not analyzed immediately (analyze within 48 hours)



6.4 DOC Analysis

Analyze filtered extracts for dissolved organic carbon using the Shimadzu TOC-L (see SOP-L06) or equivalent TOC analyzer
Run 0.5 M K2SO4 blanks alongside samples



6.5 Calculation
Microbial biomass carbon is calculated as:
\[
\text{MBC} = \frac{C_{\text{fumigated}} - C_{\text{unfumigated}}}{k_C}
\]
where:

\(C_{\text{fumigated}}\) = DOC in the fumigated extract (mg C kg-1 dry soil)
\(C_{\text{unfumigated}}\) = DOC in the unfumigated extract (mg C kg-1 dry soil)
\(k_C\) = 0.45, the extraction efficiency coefficient (Vance et al., 1987)







Note



The unfumigated extract DOC value represents the background dissolved organic carbon pool and is often reported separately as an indicator of labile soil carbon.

Run analytical triplicates for at least 10% of samples
Include a reagent blank (0.5 M K2SO4 only, no soil) in each batch
Include a laboratory reference soil in each batch to monitor method consistency
Verify that the coefficient of variation among replicates is less than 15%

title: Total Carbon – Shimadzu TOC-L with SSM-5000A
text:
6. Procedure

6.1 Instrument Startup

Verify carrier gas supply pressure (typically 200 kPa or per instrument manual)
Turn on the TOC-L main unit and allow the furnace to reach operating temperature (680 C for liquid mode)
Launch LabSolutions TOC software on the connected computer
Run a system blank check using deionized water to verify baseline stability; the blank value should be below 0.1 mg/L C



6.2 Calibration

Prepare a multi-point calibration curve using potassium hydrogen phthalate (KHP) dissolved in deionized water
Typical calibration range: 0, 1, 5, 10, 25, 50, 100 mg/L C (adjust to expected sample range)
For IC calibration (if measuring TC - IC = TOC), prepare sodium bicarbonate/carbonate standards
Run calibration standards and verify that the correlation coefficient (r2) is at least 0.999
Save the calibration curve in the software



6.3 Liquid Sample Analysis (DOC in Soil Extracts)

Filter all liquid samples through 0.45 um syringe filters or pre-combusted glass fiber filters into clean autosampler vials
For K2SO4 extracts, include 0.5 M K2SO4 blanks in the run
Select the appropriate measurement mode in the software:

NPOC mode (recommended for most soil extracts): The instrument acidifies the sample with HCl, sparges with carrier gas to remove inorganic carbon as CO2, then combusts the remaining sample at 680 C. The evolved CO2 is measured by a non-dispersive infrared (NDIR) detector.
TC-IC mode (if both total and inorganic carbon are needed): TC is measured by direct combustion; IC is measured by acidification only. TOC = TC - IC.

Load vials into the autosampler and start the run
The instrument performs replicate injections (typically 3) and reports the mean and coefficient of variation







TipTip



If K2SO4 extracts have high salt content, use the instrument’s automatic dilution function to extend catalyst and combustion tube life. Dilution factors are applied automatically to the reported concentrations.




6.4 Solid Sample Analysis (SSM-5000A)

Switch the instrument to SSM mode in the LabSolutions software
Pre-combust ceramic boats at 900 C to remove any residual carbon
Weigh 10–50 mg of dried, finely ground soil into a clean ceramic boat using an analytical balance (record mass to 0.01 mg)
For TOC measurement (removing inorganic carbon): pre-treat the sample by adding a few drops of 2 M HCl to the boat, allow to react until effervescence stops, and dry at 105 C before analysis
For TC measurement (no acid pretreatment): proceed directly
Place the ceramic boat into the SSM sample port
The SSM combusts the sample in an oxygen-rich environment at high temperature; the evolved CO2 is carried to the NDIR detector
The software reports total carbon content in mg C or as a percentage of sample mass



6.5 Instrument Shutdown

After the final sample, run 3–5 deionized water blanks to flush the system
Review all data in the software for outliers or failed injections
Export data and save the run file
If the instrument will not be used for several days, turn off the furnace and carrier gas per the instrument manual

title: Total Carbon – Shimadzu TOC-L with SSM-5000A

7. Quality Control

Run a calibration verification standard (mid-range) every 10–15 samples; acceptance criterion is within 10% of the known value
Include instrument blanks (deionized water) at the beginning, middle, and end of each run
Include method blanks (0.5 M K2SO4 for extract analyses) in each batch
Run sample duplicates at a rate of at least 1 per 10 samples
Monitor the coefficient of variation among replicate injections; re-run if CV exceeds 2% for liquid samples
Log catalyst replacement, combustion tube changes, and calibration dates in the instrument logbook

title: Soil Nitrate and Ammonium – KCl Extraction
text:
7. Procedure

7.1 Preparing 2 M KCl Solution

Weigh out 298.2 g KCl into a 2 L volumetric flask
Fill the flask approximately two-thirds full with distilled water
Place the flask on a magnetic stirrer and add a magnetic stir bar
Set the stirrer to low-medium speed and leave on for 4 hours until fully dissolved
Use a stir bar retriever to remove the magnetic stir bar
Fill the flask to the 2 L mark with distilled water and mix







TipTip



Prepare the KCl solution the day before extraction. It can be stored at room temperature in a capped container indefinitely.




7.2 Moisture Subsample

Set aside 10 g of soil from each sample for moisture determination
Place each 10 g subsample into a labeled aluminum weigh boat
Dry at 105 C for 24 hours and record the dry weight
Calculate gravimetric moisture content per SOP-L40 Soil Moisture



7.3 KCl Extraction

Dispense 40 mL of 2 M KCl solution into labeled test tubes or extraction bottles
Add 7 g of field-moist soil to each tube (the total volume should reach approximately 50 mL)
Cap the tubes securely
Place on the reciprocating shaker for 2 hours
Remove from the shaker and allow soil particles to settle for approximately 10 minutes (do not exceed 1 hour)



7.4 Filtering

Set up filter funnels with Whatman #42 filter paper over labeled specimen containers or clean test tubes
Pour the shaken solution into the funnels; do not fill above the filter paper line
Allow the solution to drain completely until only soil remains on the filter
Discard the used filter paper and soil



7.5 Extract Storage

Cap the filtered extract containers
If analysis will be completed within a few days, store at 4 C
If analysis will be delayed, freeze the extracts until analysis







Important



Extracts should be analyzed as soon as possible. Prolonged storage, even frozen, can alter NH4+ and NO3- concentrations due to microbial activity or chemical transformations.

2. Scope and Definitions

Applies to: All staff, students, and researchers handling hazardous chemicals in EA Program laboratories
Does not apply to: Radioactive materials (see separate procedures)
Location: SGM 133 and associated EA Program laboratory spaces


Key Definitions
Corrosive Chemicals: Strong acids and bases, dehydrating agents, nonmetal chlorides, and halogens. These are health hazards and present problems in handling and storage. Purchase corrosives in containers with a protective plastic coating if available. Store corrosives under the hood, on low shelving, or in storage cabinets. Gas cylinders (including lecture-sized) should not be stored in the same cabinet with corrosive liquids because of possible cylinder and valve damage. Properly segregate hazardous materials to prevent fire, explosion, or toxic gas release. Segregate acids from bases and oxidizing acids from organic acids. Separate nitric acid from other acids.
Flammable Liquids: Chemicals in a liquid state that can easily burn, classified as either flammable or combustible by their flashpoints. Flammable liquids catch fire and burn easily at normal working temperatures. Combustible liquids can burn at temperatures usually above working temperatures.
Caustic Chemicals: A range of chemicals (e.g., ammonium hydroxide, potassium hydroxide, sodium hydroxide) that are able to burn or corrode organic tissue by chemical action.
Safety Data Sheet (SDS): Each chemical we use has an SDS describing the hazards and how the material should be handled. These sheets are located on the counter next to the east entrance and in the PPE shelves near the entrance of SGM 133.

6. Procedures

6.1 Handling Glassware
Check the condition of glassware before use. Only glass in good condition should be used. Discard or send for repair glass that is broken, chipped, starred, or badly scratched. Clean glassware before sending it for repair. When picking up broken glass, use proper hand protection.


6.2 Handling and Transportation of Chemicals






Important



Many lab accidents occur while carrying chemicals from one place to another or transferring chemicals between containers. It is good practice to assume that all chemicals are potentially hazardous.


General transportation rules:

Wear appropriate PPE (minimum: safety glasses, lab coat, long pants, closed-toe shoes)
Large bottles should be carried on a cart; if no cart is available, carry bottles one at a time with two hands (one around the neck, one underneath)
Do not hook a finger through the ring on top of a bottle or attempt to pick up a bottle by the cap
A bottle transporter is the safest way to transport chemicals
When using a wheeled cart, do not place bottles near the edge; bottles should not touch each other or other glassware
Be cautious rolling carts over door sills or other obstructions
When transporting outdoors, two people must be present
Incompatible chemicals should not be carried on the same cart
Use padded or rubber bottle carriers, carts, or pails to prevent breakage
Ensure containers are properly labeled; know what to do in case of a spill
Hazardous chemicals must be attended at all times while being transported
If using an elevator, use freight-only elevators if possible; otherwise use unoccupied passenger elevators
Do not move unstable, explosive, or unusually hazardous materials

Specific chemical types:

Large quantities of concentrated mineral acids should be kept in storage rooms or cabinets for corrosive substances and transported in an approved acid bottle carrier
Organic solvents should be stored in special flammable storage areas and transported in special rubber carriers



6.3 Chemical Storage

Return every chemical to its storage location after use
Store solvents, acids, bases, reactives, oxidizers, and toxins separately
Use separate cabinets or isolated areas for incompatible chemicals; check compatibility restrictions on cabinets under fume hoods
Never store hazardous chemicals on the floor; use low shelves or cabinets with a lip on the forward edge
Shelves should be securely fastened to a wall or floor and should not be overloaded
Use compatible containers for storing chemicals or wastes; metal containers are often unsuitable for corrosive wastes and halogenated solvents
Check waste containers weekly for signs of chemical leakage
Containers should be free of rust and deformation; caps should remain securely on containers when not in immediate use
NFPA labeling should appear on cabinets and room doors at waist level or lower (to be visible in dense smoke)
All containers must be labeled with content and general hazard in compliance with Hazard Communications regulations
Flammable liquids greater than 1 liter should be kept in metal safety cans; never disable the spring-loaded closure
Metal drums for flammable chemicals should be properly grounded
Store chemicals as close as possible to the point of use; identify storage locations on an emergency floor plan posted in each work area
Only limited quantities of chemicals and solvents should be stored in the lab; large drums or multiple bottles should be stored in a central chemical storage area
Dispose of out-of-date chemicals on a periodic basis



6.4 Labeling
All containers should be dated and labeled with chemical components and hazards. The user’s name should also appear on the label. Labels on incoming containers must not be removed or defaced.
Dating is especially important for compounds with a specified shelf life, such as those that form peroxides. Chemical names must be spelled out on labels – chemical formulas, acronyms, and abbreviations are not acceptable as the only identification. Laboratory samples, including field specimens and newly synthesized compounds, must be identified as accurately as possible.

7. Chemical Spill Treatment

7.1 Initial Response






WarningSafety First




Isolate the spill area
Notify proper authorities – call Campus Safety, who will relay the message to the appropriate agency (usually the Claremont Fire Department)
Wear adequate protection – eye protection, hand protection, and respiratory protection





7.2 Identify and Treat the Spill
Determine if the spill is an acid, caustic, solvent, or other material. Select the appropriate spill control agent:

Spill-X-A for acids
Spill-X-C for caustics
Spill-X-S for solvents

Treatment steps:

Encircle and cover the spill with the appropriate agent
Mix the agent with the spill using the provided scraper

For acids and bases: a neutralization reaction will leave a paste-like substance
For solvents: adsorption is indicated by the disappearance of free liquid




7.3 Restore the Area

Test representative samples of spill residue for final pH; add more agent if necessary
Use Spill-X-S to solidify any remaining liquid; final residue should be dry and powdery
Record spill type and treatment on the labels of provided bags (e.g., “neutralized acid/base, pH = ___” or “adsorbed solvent: [name]”)
After the treatment reaction cools, use the provided scraper and pan to pick up residue and place into the labeled bag
Rinse and decontaminate utensils and the spill area

title: Hazardous Materials Handling
text:
8. Chemical Waste Disposal

8.1 Waste Containers
Containers used for accumulating hazardous waste must be in good condition, free of leaks, and compatible with the waste being stored. Waste containers should be capped and only opened when adding waste. Hazardous waste must not be placed in unwashed containers that previously held incompatible materials. Containers holding waste incompatible with nearby materials must be separated or protected by a wall, partition, or secondary containment device.


8.2 Labeling and Manifests
Before chemicals can be disposed of, a waste tag must be filled out by the waste generator and attached to each container. A packing manifest must also be attached to each box, including lab information and waste information. The generator should check the manifest, sign their name, and attach it. Keep a copy for lab records.


8.3 Waste Minimization
Avoid buying and using large quantities when not necessary. Whenever possible, substitute nonhazardous, biodegradable chemicals for hazardous chemicals.


8.4 Flammable Organic Solvents
Flammable organics can often be reused for fuel unless they are extremely toxic or produce toxic combustion products. Halogenated solvents, acutely toxic flammables, acids, bases, heavy metals, oxidizers, and pesticides should be collected in separate containers.
Compounds most suitable for recovery include: acetone, 2-butanol, butyl alcohol, cyclohexane, diethyl ether, ethyl acetate, ethyl alcohol, heptane, hexane, methyl alcohol, methyl cellosolve, pentane, petroleum ether, 2-propanol, sec-butyl alcohol, tert-butyl alcohol, tetrahydrofuran, and xylene. Do not combine any of these with other chemicals.


8.5 Sink Disposal
Very few chemical wastes are acceptable for disposal down the sink or sanitary sewer system. Small-scale research activities (100 mL or less) of certain water-soluble, nontoxic, and nonflammable chemicals may be poured only if approved by the Chemical Safety Director.


8.6 Waste Packing Procedure

Collect each chemical waste in a separate screw-top container; do not mix wastes
Use the smallest container size to match the amount of waste generated
Waste containers should be securely capped and labeled with chemical content (for mixtures, give approximate percentages)
Completely fill waste collection containers
Shock-sensitive and water-reactive compounds require special handling and should be packed separately
Determine the packing hazard class for each waste, prioritizing reactivity over toxicity
Segregate wastes by hazard class and pack into separate cardboard boxes
Place dividers and shock-absorbing materials (newspaper, vermiculite) between containers
Specify where the waste is to be picked up

title: Hazardous Materials Handling
text:
9. Lessons Learned






NoteLearning from Past Incidents



History provides many instances of laboratory safety breakdowns. By analyzing the causes of laboratory accidents, we can identify patterns that lead to both positive and negative safety outcomes.


Cuts: Dispose of all sharp metal and glass properly. Inspect glassware for cracks prior to use. Use extreme care around glass in the lab.
Burns: Minimize fire hazard by using hot plates or water baths instead of open flames. Tie up loose hair and wear snug clothing, avoiding synthetic materials when possible. Always use a fume hood when working with volatile organic compounds.
Chemical spills: Read the SDS before working with any hazardous chemical. Always wear PPE, cap unused chemical containers, and use engineering controls such as fume hoods when necessary. Never work alone in the laboratory.
Mercury spills: Follow the college’s emergency instructions for mercury spill response.
Explosions: Develop written protocols for handling explosive chemicals. Use fume hoods, avoid carrying out experiments in closed containers, and use PPE.
Chemical inhalation: Never breathe deeply from a chemical mixture. In addition to working in a fume hood, consider using equipment that can monitor gas levels from an experiment.

6. Health and Safety

6.1 General Safety Rules

Developing a safe and productive environment is key to sustaining a strong scientific ethic; reflect on how you and your colleagues can promote safe conditions

7. Emergency Procedures






ImportantEmergency Numbers




Campus Safety: (909) 607-2000 (from a campus phone, dial x72000) – open 24/7
Emergency: 911
Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222
CUC Student Health Services: 909-621-8222

When calling Campus Safety, be ready to provide your name, the location of the emergency, and your contact phone number. Campus Safety will assess the situation and call any necessary services (ambulance, fire department, etc.).
Pomona College On-Call Deans and the Monsour On-Call Counselor are reachable via Campus Safety’s emergency number.



7.1 Earthquakes
Earthquakes are common in southern California. Developing an effective strategy before an earthquake strikes is key to laboratory safety.
Indoor response:

Move away from windows, filing cabinets, shelves, chemicals, and other heavy objects that may fall
“Duck, Cover, and Hold” until shaking stops
If not near a table or sturdy desk, crouch against an interior wall and cover your neck and head
Once shaking stops, take any necessary items (phone, wallet, medication) and leave the building
Go to the nearest Pomona College evacuation site and wait for further instructions
Put on shoes as there could be broken debris
DO NOT USE ELEVATORS

Outdoor response:

Move away from buildings, trees, signs, electrical poles, and wires
Protect your head and neck
After shaking stops, go to the nearest evacuation site

Aftershocks may occur. Be prepared and follow appropriate evacuation plans if they do.


7.2 Fires and Evacuation
In the case of a small fire, you may attempt to use a fire extinguisher. Remember:

Remove people from the area
Activate the closest fire alarm
Call Campus Safety
Extinguish the fire only if safe to do so:

Place yourself between the fire and the exit
Pull the pin
Aim the nozzle toward the base of the fire
Squeeze the handle to release the extinguishing agent
Sweep the base of the fire from side to side

Use only one fire extinguisher; if the fire is not controlled after one, leave the room, close the door, and evacuate

If trapped in a building:

Call Campus Safety
Close all windows and doors
Wet and place cloth material around and under the door to prevent smoke from entering



7.3 Medical Emergencies

Call Campus Safety; let them know the victim’s condition
Provide necessary first aid until Campus Safety and/or emergency services arrive (only if trained)
Do not move the injured person unless necessary
See the campus evacuation map for AED locations



7.4 Chemical Spills
If there is a hazardous chemical spill in the laboratory, do not attempt to clean it up unless trained and equipped to do so. Refer to SOP-L02 Hazardous Materials Handling for spill response procedures.

If chemicals get in your eye, flush for 15 minutes at the eyewash station
If toxic materials are spilled on your body, remove all clothing and stand beneath the lab shower for 15 minutes
In the event of inhalation, move to fresh air
If someone is at risk, protect yourself first; only provide assistance if you can do so safely



7.5 Crime on Campus
Active shooter: Exit the building if safe to do so. If not, close and lock the laboratory door, turn off lights, pull down window shades, keep quiet, silence phones, and call Campus Safety.
Bomb threat and utilities failure: Review the Emergency Brochure posted near laboratory exits for detailed procedures.

title: Soil Moisture – Gravimetric Method
text:
7. Procedure

7.1 Preparation

Print copies of the Soil Moisture Datasheet (Appendix A) for recording measurements
Label aluminum tins or ceramic crucibles with a permanent marker or engraving tool
Pre-dry the empty containers at 105 C for at least 1 hour to remove any residual moisture
Cool the containers in a desiccator to room temperature
Weigh each empty container to the nearest 0.01 g and record as Tin Weight on the datasheet



7.2 Sample Weighing

Using a spatula, transfer approximately 10–20 g of field-moist soil into a pre-weighed container
Record the mass of the container plus moist soil to the nearest 0.01 g as Wet Weight on the datasheet
Avoid compacting the soil in the container; a loose arrangement promotes even drying







TipTip



Process moisture subsamples at the same time as other subsamples (e.g., for microbial biomass or respiration) to ensure the moisture value accurately reflects the condition of the soil used in those analyses.




7.3 Drying

Place the uncovered containers in the drying oven set to 105 C
Dry for a minimum of 24 hours
After 24 hours, remove one or two containers, cool in the desiccator, and re-weigh. If the mass has decreased by more than 0.01 g compared to a check 2 hours earlier, return all samples to the oven for an additional 4 hours and re-check
Drying is complete when the mass is constant (change of less than 0.01 g between successive weighings)



7.4 Cooling and Final Weighing

Transfer all containers from the oven to a desiccator
Allow to cool to room temperature (approximately 20–30 minutes)
Weigh each container plus dry soil to the nearest 0.01 g and record as Dry Weight on the datasheet



7.5 Calculations
Gravimetric soil moisture content (%):
\[
\theta_g (\%) = \left( \frac{W_{\text{moist}} - W_{\text{dry}}}{W_{\text{dry}} - W_{\text{container}}} \right) \times 100
\]
where:

\(W_{\text{moist}}\) = mass of container + moist soil (g)
\(W_{\text{dry}}\) = mass of container + oven-dried soil (g)
\(W_{\text{container}}\) = mass of empty container (g)

Dry-weight correction factor (for converting field-moist analytical results to a dry-weight basis):
\[
f = \frac{W_{\text{moist}} - W_{\text{container}}}{W_{\text{dry}} - W_{\text{container}}}
\]
To convert a result expressed per gram of moist soil to per gram of dry soil, multiply by \(f\).

title: Soil Moisture – Gravimetric Method
text:
8. Quality Control

Run analytical duplicates for at least 10% of samples; the coefficient of variation between duplicates should be less than 5%
Verify oven temperature with a calibrated thermometer at the start of each drying cycle
Ensure the desiccator contains active (indicating) desiccant; replace or regenerate when the indicator changes color
Re-weigh a subset of samples after an additional 2 hours of drying to confirm mass constancy

title: Soil Organic Matter – Loss on Ignition
text:
6. Procedure

6.1 Crucible Preparation

Pre-combust all ceramic crucibles in the muffle furnace at 550 C for 1 hour to remove any residual organic material
Cool crucibles in a desiccator to room temperature
Weigh each empty crucible to the nearest 0.0001 g and record as \(W_{\text{crucible}}\)



6.2 Drying at 105 C

Add approximately 5 g of air-dried, sieved (2 mm) soil to a pre-weighed crucible
Record the exact mass of crucible + soil
Place crucibles in the drying oven at 105 C for 24 hours
Remove crucibles, cool in a desiccator, and weigh to the nearest 0.0001 g
Record as \(W_{105}\) (mass of oven-dried soil, excluding crucible)







TipTip



If the mass has not stabilized (i.e., decreases by more than 0.001 g on re-weighing), return the sample to the oven for an additional 2–4 hours and re-weigh.




6.3 Combustion at 550 C

Transfer the crucibles containing oven-dried soil directly into the muffle furnace
Ramp the furnace to 550 C (if programmable, use a ramp rate of approximately 10 C per minute)
Hold at 550 C for 4 hours
Turn off the furnace and allow crucibles to cool inside the furnace until they can be safely transferred (below approximately 200 C)
Transfer crucibles to a desiccator and cool to room temperature
Weigh to the nearest 0.0001 g
Record as \(W_{550}\) (mass of combusted soil, excluding crucible)



6.4 Calculation
Soil organic matter content is calculated as:
\[
\text{SOM (\%)} = \left( \frac{W_{105} - W_{550}}{W_{105}} \right) \times 100
\]
where:

\(W_{105}\) = mass of oven-dried soil (g)
\(W_{550}\) = mass of soil after combustion at 550 C (g)

Run analytical duplicates for at least 10% of samples; coefficient of variation should be less than 5%
Include an empty crucible blank in each furnace run to verify no mass gain from ambient contamination
Include a laboratory reference soil with known SOM in each batch
Verify oven (105 C) and furnace (550 C) temperatures using a calibrated thermometer or thermocouple at regular intervals

text:
6. Procedure

6.1 Sample Preparation

Use field-moist soil that has been sieved through a 2 mm sieve per SOP-F02
Samples should be stored at 4 C and processed within 48 hours of collection



6.2 Incubation Setup

Weigh approximately 40 g of field-moist soil into a clean incubation jar
Record the exact mass of soil added
Add the specified volume of deionized water according to the Solvita protocol (the rewetting triggers the microbial CO2 burst)
Insert a fresh CO2-sensitive gel paddle into the jar, ensuring the gel faces the soil surface
Seal the jar immediately and securely
Record the jar number, sample ID, and start time



6.3 Incubation

Place sealed jars in the incubator set to 25 C
Incubate undisturbed for 24 hours
Do not open or move jars during incubation



6.4 Reading Results

After exactly 24 hours, remove the gel paddle from the jar
Immediately read the paddle using the Solvita Digital Color Reader
Record the color number and corresponding CO2-C value
Express results as mg CO2-C kg-1 soil







TipTip



Read paddles promptly after removing them from the jar. Prolonged exposure to ambient air will alter the gel color and compromise the reading.




6.5 Cleanup

Dispose of used soil in the designated waste container
Wash incubation jars thoroughly with soap and water; rinse with deionized water
Dispose of used gel paddles in standard trash
crumbs: Soil Respiration -- Solvita CO2 Burst Test

title: Soil Respiration – Solvita CO2 Burst Test
text:
7. Quality Control

Run duplicate samples at a rate of 1 per 10 to assess analytical precision
Include a blank jar (empty, sealed with gel paddle) in each batch to check for background CO2
Verify incubator temperature at the start and end of each 24-hour incubation period
Calibrate the Digital Color Reader according to manufacturer instructions before each batch
crumbs: Soil Respiration -- Solvita CO2 Burst Test

title: Soil Respiration – Solvita CO2 Burst Test
text:
8. Data Interpretation
The CO2 burst is proportional to microbial biomass and is directly tied to potential carbon and nitrogen mineralization. Typical values for agricultural soils range from approximately 10 to 200+ mg CO2-C kg-1 soil, with higher values indicating greater microbial activity and labile carbon availability.

text: This SOP covers field-based research activities and class field trips, addressing transportation, weather-based, and biotic hazards. Although we cannot predict all risks and hazards, it is everyone’s responsibility to identify and mitigate potential risks associated with field work.

text:

Anyone conducting research in the field is required to have documented training before commencing field work. Learning about risks and taking the precautions described here is the first step to reducing the risks associated with field work. Anyone working in the field should identify potential risks and attempt to mitigate them.

title: Field Safety
text:
4. Safety and Hazards






WarningGeneral Field Hazards



Reducing risks is one of our main priorities. Like many endeavors in life, field work has certain risks. However, we can reduce these risks dramatically by understanding our physical limits and how these can be tested by uncontrolled environmental factors.
We rely on each individual to be mindful of their own limitations and to advocate for themselves and others to reduce risk exposure.



Required Materials

First Aid Kit (kits are located in EA vehicles; see EA vehicle checklist to document their presence)
Cell phone(s)
Walkie-talkies (optional)
Personal Protective Equipment (PPE)



Estimated Time
Preparing to go in the field can take a few minutes to several hours of planning and gathering resources. A good rule of thumb is to double the time you think it will take to get ready.

title: Field Safety
text:
5. Transportation Safety

5.1 Vehicle Requirements

Drivers must have valid driver’s licenses and insurance
Drivers using EA vehicles must be approved by the college; forms can be found in the EA Department



5.2 Planning

Identify meet-up and departure times and locations
Designate a driver
All state and local laws must be obeyed



5.3 Responding to Vehicle Emergencies
Refer to the college’s vehicle emergency procedures. Ensure all occupants are safe, call emergency services if needed, and report the incident to the EA Department.

title: Field Safety
text:
6. Weather-Related Hazards

6.1 Heat Exhaustion and Stroke






WarningRisk Factors




Working outside of shade in desert or arid climates, especially during hot times of day
Lack of shade coverage or proper sun protection
Dehydration



Prevention:

Use and reapply sunscreen
Drink plenty of water
Wear hats and other protective clothing

Response:

Hydrate the affected person
Place ice packs on neck, armpits, etc.
If conditions worsen, leave the field and find air-conditioned conditions



6.2 Cold Conditions
Risk factors: Lack of sun, time of year, wind chill
Prevention: Proper layering and clothing; stay hydrated
Response: Eat, evacuate to warmth, get a professional evaluation


6.3 Lightning
Prevention: Check weather forecast; learn to identify cumulonimbus clouds
Response: Assume lightning position and seek shelter immediately; avoid open areas, tall isolated trees, and bodies of water


6.4 Air Quality and Pollution
Working outside when ozone levels or other pollutants are elevated has a detrimental effect on health, particularly for individuals with asthma or other respiratory conditions. Hot, dry days worsen pollution, and nearby forest fires degrade air quality.
Students with any respiratory disease should be cautious and report the condition to their instructor or laboratory supervisor.
Prevention: Check air quality index (AQI) before field work; postpone if AQI is unhealthy
Response: Leave the field if symptoms develop; seek medical attention if needed

title: Field Safety
text:
7. Geological and Environmental Hazards

7.1 Earthquake
Tectonic movement may occur anywhere in California.
Prevention: Be aware of surroundings at all times
Response: Remain low to the ground; stay away from external building frames; avoid sinkholes, gas lines, and utility wires


7.2 Flooding
Risk factors: Proximity to bodies of water, excessive rainfall
Prevention: Check the forecast for rainfall; be aware of surroundings
Response: Find the highest point in the area; do not attempt to cross rushing water


7.3 Altitude Illness (HAPE/HACE)
Risk factors: High altitudes to which students have not had time to acclimate; reduced oxygen
Symptoms: Headache, nausea, irritability
Response: If mild symptoms, acclimate and take it easy; hydrate. If persistent vomiting and severe headache, evacuate to lower altitude immediately.


7.4 Human Debris and Waste
Illegal dumping of waste and leftover construction materials (sharp metallic objects, etc.) bring risk of injury and exposure to long-term illnesses like tetanus.
Prevention: Avoid and report; be aware of surroundings; think before interacting with unusual objects
Response: Students should be aware of their vaccination history and how to proceed if they require a tetanus shot due to injury


7.5 Toxic Waste Exposure
Exposure may occur via ingestion, inhalation, or dermal contact and can be unpredictable.
Prevention: Wear appropriate PPE; avoid contact with unknown substances
Response: Remove from exposure; decontaminate; seek medical attention

title: Field Safety
text:
8. Biotic Hazards
The field is home to a vast diversity of organisms. Being respectful of their environment is crucial to their safety and our own.

8.1 Allergies






Important



All allergies must be recorded in medical files before the start of field work. Researchers with life-threatening allergies must bring their Epi-pen to the field and keep it accessible at all times.


Mild allergic reaction: Administer 25–50 mg of Diphenhydramine (Benadryl)
Severe allergic reaction (swelling of face/throat, respiratory distress): Administer 0.3 mg of Epinephrine; may re-administer after 5 minutes. Follow with 25–50 mg of Diphenhydramine and 20–40 mg of Prednisone. Evacuate from field site immediately.


8.2 Biotic Risk Summary









Organism
Habitats
Risks
Prevention and Response

Near stagnant water
Vectors for disease (e.g., Malaria)
Use mosquito repellent (e.g., DEET products)

9. Other Illness and Injury

9.1 Fractures and Breaks
Stabilize the injured area and avoid movement. Go to the nearest medical facility for further care.


9.2 Injury from Equipment
Handle all equipment with caution. Carefully read operating procedures. Seek help from fellow students or your instructor if you have questions or doubts. Do not use any equipment if you are unsure of how to handle it.


9.3 Chronic Conditions (Epilepsy, Diabetes, Heart Conditions)
Refer to emergency procedures. Report any chronic conditions to your supervisor. Be aware of your surroundings and be prepared to react in an emergency. Know where the first aid kit is and how to get to the nearest medical facility.

8. Interferences

Calibration is essential for obtaining meaningful data. Always calibrate before each field outing.
The reference electrode must be maintained by refilling the reference electrolyte once every few months. Failure to do so causes unreliable pH readings.
When sampling in streams or rivers, take downstream measurements first to avoid your movements and presence affecting the readings. Stand on the bank or downstream of the measurement point while the probe is in the water.

text:
9. Pre-Field Preparation

9.1 Charging
Charge the Amphibian 2 portable PC before going into the field. The charger plugs into the round hole on the bottom edge of the Amphibian. Allow several hours or charge overnight.


9.2 Probe Setup for Calibration

Remove the blue storage plug from the probe and cover the plug with a plastic protector
Insert the underwater cable to connect the Amphibian and the Manta2
Turn on the Amphibian by pressing the power button (bottom right corner)
Press the Windows icon (lower left), then select Amp_2_2_6 (or use shortcut button P1)
Once the interface loads, press “Manta2” on the lower left bar and select “Calibrate”



9.3 pH Calibration (Three-Point)

Select “pH units” from the Manta2 calibration menu
Input the value of your first standard (e.g., 7.00) in the unshaded box
Unscrew the blue cap from the larger cap, leaving the clear plastic cup around the sensors in place
Pour a small amount of the first standard into the cup (probe facing upward), cap it, and shake to rinse the sensors. Repeat twice, pouring used standard into a waste beaker each time
Fill the cup with approximately 1 inch of the standard
Wait for the red line on the Amphibian chart to stabilize (flatten), then press “Ok”
When prompted for the second standard, rinse twice with DI water, then twice with the second standard, fill to 1 inch, and repeat
Select the option for three-point calibration and repeat with the third standard
Accept the calibration when the SRF falls within the acceptable range (consult Prof. Los Huertos if uncertain)



9.4 Conductivity Calibration (One-Point)

Rinse the probe twice with DI water to remove any residual pH standard
Tap “Manta2” > “Calibrate” > “spCond mS/cm”
Input 2.765 in the unshaded box
Rinse twice with conductivity standard, then fill the cup to 1 inch
Wait for the red line to stabilize, then press “Ok”
The SRF should be approximately 110–120. If outside this range, recalibrate. If still outside the range after recalibration, contact Prof. Los Huertos







Note



Conductivity standard can be disposed of down the drain. pH standards must go in a waste container.




9.5 Dissolved Oxygen Calibration
Prepare air-saturated water:

Put approximately half a liter of tap water in a liter jar
Shake the jar vigorously for one minute with the lid on
Remove the lid and let the water stand for about five minutes to allow air bubbles to escape

Calibrate HDO %sat:

Rinse the probe twice with DI water
If the circulator is on (check next to “Manta2”), set it to “CircOff”
Tap “Manta2” > “Calibrate” > “HDO %sat”
Input the barometric pressure for your location in mm Hg (find on an online weather station; convert units if needed; round to 3 significant figures)
When prompted to reset HDO to factory settings, select “No”
Fill the calibration cup with aerated water until it covers the sensors by approximately 1 cm
Wait a few minutes for temperature to equilibrate; the reading must be stable for 3 minutes
Press “Ok” to accept. The SRF should be 100. If it differs, redo the calibration. If still not 100, contact Prof. Los Huertos.

Calibrate HDO mg/L:

Immediately after %sat calibration, note the temperature on the snapshot screen
Tap “Manta2” > “Calibrate” > “HDO mg/L”
Use a DO saturation calculator (e.g., waterontheweb.org) to convert %sat to mg/L using the temperature and pressure values
Input the mg/L value as your calibration standard
Wait 20 seconds for the readout to stabilize. If stable, press “Ok”
If the value changes significantly, exit, re-read %sat, and use the new value to recalibrate mg/L

10. Field Procedure

10.1 Connecting and Powering On

Connect the Manta2 to the Amphibian via the underwater cable
Power on the Amphibian and launch Amp_2_2_6 (shortcut: P1)
Adjust screen brightness using arrow up + P3 (dimmer) and arrow up + P4 (brighter)



10.2 Enabling GPS

Tap on the GPS/GNSS status gadget
A satellite icon will appear on the top bar while searching
Do not cover the top cap (antenna) during satellite acquisition
Wait until satellites are found (check: 5 SV = 5 satellites; 3Diff/4 satellites for 3D fix; lower PDOP = better accuracy)
Enable GPS at least 5 minutes before taking readings



10.3 Taking Measurements

Place the weighted protective cap over the sensors
Lower the probe into the water at the measurement point
Allow the probe to equilibrate for at least 2 minutes before reading
Take a snapshot using the top-left button on the Main screen
Annotate the file using the format: Year.Month.Day.Project (e.g., 2026.05.13.StreampH)







TipTip



In flowing water, always measure downstream sites first, then work upstream to avoid disturbing the water at your measurement locations.




10.4 Disconnecting

Remove the probe from the water
Disconnect the underwater cable from the probe
Insert the blue storage plug
Cover the cable end with the plastic protector

11. Post-Field Procedures

11.1 Cleaning the Probe

Clean the probe with warm soapy water (liquid dish soap or mild household cleaner)
Clean sensor stems with a soft brush
Rinse thoroughly with tap water
Store sensors with tap water inside the cup



11.2 Downloading Data

Connect the Amphibian to your PC using a USB cable
A green window will appear with four options; select “File Management”
In the next window, navigate to the hard drive, then select “My Documents”
Locate the Excel document with your data
Copy the file to your project data folder



11.3 Charging
Return the Amphibian to its charging station after each field outing.

12. Troubleshooting







Problem
Solution




No power
Check the green LED on the Manta2; if off, the voltage is insufficient. Try another cable.


pH SRF out of range
Recalibrate with fresh standards. If still out of range, refill the reference electrolyte and contact Prof. Los Huertos.


Conductivity SRF outside 110–120
Recalibrate. If still out of range, contact Prof. Los Huertos.


HDO %sat SRF not 100
Redo the calibration with freshly aerated water.


GPS not acquiring satellites
Ensure the top cap (antenna) is uncovered; move to an open area away from overhead obstructions.
